title: How Stuntmen (and -women) Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the history and craft of movie stunt people (stunt men and women). They cover early slapstick stunts with Buster Keaton, the development of stunt technology (squibs, air rams, airbags, process trailers), CGI replacing some stunts, safety on set and the assistant director's role, the stunt coordinator and second unit director, stage fighting, gunshot effects and the Brandon Lee shooting, fire stunts, falls (including Dar Robinson's Sharky's Machine fall), how to break into stunt work, schools and books, and actors who do their own stunts. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about the hosts' verbal tics and promotion of the Science Channel TV show.
topics: actors who do their own stunts

segments.title: Opening banter and The Fall Guy
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the show's intro and the 1980s TV show The Fall Guy, noting its portrayal of a moonlighting stuntman who is bitter about lack of glory.

segments.title: Anonymity and awards for stunt people
segments.summary: They note stunt people rarely get recognition; the Academy has no stunt category, though Emmys and the Taurus World Stunt Awards exist. The hosts could not find information on a 2011 Taurus awards event.

segments.title: Defining stunt people and early history
segments.summary: They distinguish movie stunt people from extreme sport athletes and rodeo riders, describe the goal of making staged action look real, and note stunt women and cross-dressing men in early film.

segments.title: Buster Keaton and early stunts
segments.summary: Early stunts were done by slapstick comedians such as Buster Keaton, whose Steamboat Bill, Jr. has a famous falling facade scene. Early stunts were often real, dangerous acts.

segments.title: Growth of the stunt profession and technology
segments.summary: As westerns and action films grew, specialized stunt performers emerged. In the sixties and seventies, technologies like squibs, air rams, airbags and roll cages developed; CGI later replaced some stunts.

segments.title: CGI, Harrison Ford and safety
segments.summary: The hosts criticize CGI in Kingdom of the Crystal Skull, where Harrison Ford's stunt was replaced by CGI. They say safety has improved but risk remains, and that actors cannot always do stunts.

segments.title: Why studios hire stunt people
segments.summary: Stunt people are hired for skills and safety, and for financial reasons such as using doubles or second units to shoot simultaneously. Process trailers and poor man's process are explained as techniques for filming car scenes.

segments.title: Actors doing their own stunts
segments.summary: Actors may train for certain skills, but it is usually more practical to hire stunt people. Tom Cruise is mentioned as someone who does many of his own stunts.

segments.title: Stunt safety, accidents and set regulations
segments.summary: Union rules have made stunts safer, but injuries and deaths still occur. The hosts discuss the Hell's Angels deaths and the Twilight Zone: The Movie helicopter tragedy. The assistant director is responsible for safety and must show fake guns to the crew.

segments.title: Pay and working conditions
segments.summary: Stunt people earn a decent rate but work is scarce, with much competition. Hours are long because stunts are rehearsed and measured repeatedly.

segments.title: Stunt coordinators and second unit directors
segments.summary: The stunt coordinator hires, plans and oversees stunts, and is a department head. Second unit directors are often former stunt people or coordinators.

segments.title: Stage fighting and staged punches
segments.summary: Stage fighting training is essential for stunt people. Punches are sold with camera angles and sound effects, and stunt performers may be launched by ramps.

segments.title: Squibs, bullet holes and blanks
segments.summary: Squibs are blood packets rigged over a protective chest plate, and bullet holes are made with pre-drilled holes covered with putty or paper. Tarantino reportedly used real squibs. Blanks contain gunpowder and wads and can be dangerous; Brandon Lee died when a bullet lodged in the barrel of a gun on The Crow fired.

segments.title: Falls and air bags
segments.summary: Falls were historically done onto large air bags, now often replaced by bungee rigs. Cardboard boxes are sometimes used for short falls. Dar Robinson's fall through a window in Sharky's Machine onto an air bag from about 150 feet is discussed.

segments.title: Stunt people's temperament
segments.summary: Stunt people are sensible and focused on safety despite their dangerous work, and talking with them can be less exciting than expected.

segments.title: Fire stunts and explosions
segments.summary: Fire stunts use fire-retardant clothing, hoods with oxygen, and flammable gel, with timing carefully set. Explosions are sometimes enhanced by force perspective and air rams, as in Commando. Anchorman's street brawl fire is referenced.

segments.title: Stunt driving and breaking into stunt work
segments.summary: The movie Hooper is discussed as a stunt-themed film. Advice on becoming a stunt person: start as an extra and befriend the stunt coordinator or second unit director, with no degree required. Stunt schools like International Stunt School and Rick Seaman Stunt Driving School are mentioned. Specialized skills help.

segments.title: Books about stunts
segments.summary: Books mentioned include So You Want to Be a Stuntman by Mark Aspitt, The Full Burn by Kevin Conley, Fight Choreography by John Kring, and Hal Needham's autobiography Stuntman!.

segments.title: Actors who perform their own stunts
segments.summary: Jason Statham, Zoe Bell (hanging on the hood in Death Proof), Burt Reynolds, Burt Lancaster, Harrison Ford, Angelina Jolie, Cameron Diaz, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Jackie Chan and others are noted for doing stunts. Joe Canutt's chariot race save for Charlton Heston in Ben-Hur is described.

segments.title: Tom Cruise stunts and Haywire
segments.summary: Tom Cruise's climbing stunt on a mountain is discussed, including a late arrival at a Moab shoot. Gina Carano's stunts in Haywire are described.

segments.title: Listener mail: verbal tics
segments.summary: A listener lists words and phrases the hosts overuse, including like, bon Jovi, and I E E G. The hosts respond and comment on their habits.

segments.title: Show promotion and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts promote the Science Channel TV show premiering Saturday at 10 pm, and iTunes availability, then give social media and email contact info.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts sign off with the closing credits and HowStuffWorks reference.
